metadata.title: The Hard Case
metadata.purpose: Take the easier-task reflex apart on one problem — 17 ÷ 5, three tiers, one hard case — and land the carry-out that differentiation flexes the door in and refuses to touch the room behind it. The design trade-off worth naming: tiering optimizes for who gets to the concept; what it refuses to sacrifice is the concept itself. Cognitive load theory is the reason the rule survives — germane load is the curriculum; strip it out and you have not simplified, you have deleted.

beats.narration_text: The reflex: student struggles, make the task easier. Watch what that quietly deletes — the thinking you were trying to build. So what actually changes: the task itself, or just the door in?

props.text:
My strugglers cannot
do this. So I will make
their task easier?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('easier' -> 'different') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Take it apart on one problem: seventeen divided by five. Three tiers, and I want you to watch what changed and what refused to change. Below tier — draw seventeen dots, group them by five, circle the two left over. At tier — three, remainder two, a basket analogy: two apples left. Above tier — the same equation, then a proof: why must the remainder always be smaller than the divisor? Three different doors into the same room. Here is the design move worth naming: the representation flexes, the entry point flexes, but the hard case — the remainder — sits inside every tier. Nobody got a simpler problem. That is not a shortcut being denied; that is the whole point of the mechanism.

shot.new_visual_element: Three tier cards (Below/At/Above) on 17 ÷ 5, all converging on one 'remainder = 2' card

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — three doors, one remainder
production_viz.mechanic: Three stacked cards (Below: dots grouped by 5, 2 circled; At: 3 R2 basket line; Above: proof prompt) each send a line down to one shared card reading REMAINDER = 2, which lights up terracotta. THIS EXACT ANCHOR (the remainder card) RETURNS AT B04.

beats.narration_text: That is the general rule the mechanism is enforcing. Differentiation flexes the scaffold, the representation, the entry point — and refuses to touch the intellectual demand. Watch what happens when the rule bends. Give a struggling reader a simpler book: today's lesson works, and next month's gap widens, because they never once practiced the hard case. Give them the same text with more support instead: same book, different scaffold, real shot at closing that gap. Same trade-off the tiers made — flex the door, protect the room. What this design optimizes for is who gets in; what it refuses to sacrifice is what happens once they are there.

shot.new_visual_element: A simpler book (struck, gap grows) beside the same book plus scaffold (gap closes)

production_viz.label: Simpler book, growing gap — same book, closing gap
production_viz.mechanic: Left card: SIMPLER BOOK, a gap bar that grows and turns terracotta over a NEXT MONTH label. Right card: SAME BOOK + SCAFFOLD, the same gap bar shrinking to near zero. A bottom line reads SAME BOOK. DIFFERENT SCAFFOLD.

beats.narration_text: Here is the one-question test that tells you which system you are actually running. Ask: does every tier arrive at the same place? Three doors into one room — differentiation, and the design holds. One entry forking into three separate ceilings, where the below-tier task caps out lower than the rest — that is tracking, even if the scaffolding on the way in looked kind. The tell is the exit, not the entrance. Widening the path keeps everyone in the room. Forking it means some students never reach the room at all. Same paperwork, opposite outcome — which is why the test has to look past intent.

shot.new_visual_element: Two columns: 3 arrows converging on 1 room (differentiation) vs 1 entry forking into 3 capped ceilings (tracking)

production_viz.label: One room, or three ceilings?
production_viz.mechanic: Left column DIFFERENTIATION: three labelled arrows (Below/At/Above) converge into one card, SAME ROOM, lit terracotta. Right column TRACKING: one entry forks into three boxes each capped by a flat lid, one lid drawn visibly lower than the others. Caption under each: 'holds' / 'even from a good scaffold, this is tracking'.

beats.narration_text: Cognitive load theory tells you why the rule survives contact with a real classroom. It splits the work into two piles. Extraneous load is waste — confusing formats, clutter, extra steps — and the scaffold's whole job is to absorb it. Germane load is the actual grappling with the concept, and that pile is the curriculum. Go back to seventeen divided by five: the remainder is germane load. Strip it out to make the task easier and you have not simplified anything — you have deleted the lesson. That is the trade-off the easier-task instinct never sees: the piece it is proud of removing is the piece worth keeping.

shot.new_visual_element: Two piles, EXTRANEOUS (absorbed by scaffold) and GERMANE (kept by learner); the REMAINDER = 2 anchor card drops into GERMANE

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — the remainder is germane load
production_viz.mechanic: Two piles side by side: EXTRANEOUS LOAD (clutter icons, an arrow into a card labelled SCAFFOLD ABSORBS) and GERMANE LOAD (an arrow into a card labelled LEARNER KEEPS). THE B01 REMAINDER = 2 CARD RETURNS, identical, and drops into the GERMANE pile. A struck line reads 'strip it out -> not simplified. deleted.'

beats.narration_text: Differentiation changes the door in — never the hard case waiting behind it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Take a lesson you already teach. Tell it the main concept and the hard case — the exact moment students get stuck. Ask it to design three tiers — concrete, representational, and abstract — all keeping that same hard case intact. Then compare the three side by side and audit whether the intellectual demand actually matches across every tier. Go deeper: now ask the model to draft a tracked version of the same lesson that quietly makes the below-tier task easier by removing the hard case, and to name exactly what got deleted — that is the germane load your differentiated version was protecting.

llm_exercise.prompt: I teach [your lesson topic]. The main concept is [X] and the hard case — the exact moment where my students consistently get stuck — is [Y]. Design three differentiation tiers for this lesson: concrete (manipulatives or physical modeling), representational (a diagram or visual analogy), and abstract (the symbolic or fully formal version). All three tiers must keep hard case Y intact — do not remove it, do not route around it. Then present the three tiers side by side and audit each one: does the intellectual demand actually match across all three, or did a tier quietly get easier?
